explanations.explanation: Jeremiah, the prophet who is praying here, says it right up front: “You have made the heavens and the earth by Your great power and outstretched arm.” (Jeremiah 32:17) Babylon's army is outside, and he starts with who God is. I think that's a man who knows where to look first. Friend, that's some steady knees.

No walls show up in this part of the prayer, friend. Jeremiah says God made the heavens and the earth by His great power and outstretched arm (Jeremiah 32:17). A wall is a small thing next to the sky overhead and the ground under your feet. Easy to grab a famous wall when you're thinking big, though.

A tower isn't in Jeremiah's prayer. He says God made the heavens and the earth by His great power and outstretched arm (Jeremiah 32:17). That's the whole sky and the whole ground, baker. No tower is going to compete with that.

Jeremiah says the opposite. Right after he praises God for making the heavens and the earth, he says, “Nothing is too difficult for You!” (Jeremiah 32:17) Not a few things, baker. Nothing. I'd read that one twice, because it's the line the whole passage leans on.
That's right, baker. Jeremiah doesn't give God a short list of hard jobs. He says, “Nothing is too difficult for You!” (Jeremiah 32:17) He says it with the enemy camped around the city, too.

explanations.answer: To reward each one by his ways
explanations.explanation: Jeremiah says God's eyes are on all the ways of the sons of men, “…to reward each one according to his ways and according to the fruit of his deeds.” (Jeremiah 32:19) So He's looking at each person's own ways. Not a crowd, not an average. Each one.

explanations.answer: To find the ones He can trust
explanations.explanation: That's a nice thought, but it isn't what Jeremiah says. His prayer says God's eyes are on all the ways of the sons of men, “…to reward each one according to his ways and according to the fruit of his deeds.” (Jeremiah 32:19) The verse gives a reason, and trust-hunting isn't it. Go with what the verse says, friend.

explanations.answer: To keep count of every name
explanations.explanation: Jeremiah doesn't mention a name count here, baker. He says God's eyes are on all the ways of people, “…to reward each one according to his ways and according to the fruit of his deeds.” (Jeremiah 32:19) It's about what each one does, not a roll call. Nobody's holding a clipboard in this verse.

explanations.answer: The land He swore to their fathers
explanations.explanation: Jeremiah says, “You gave them this land that You had sworn to give their fathers, a land flowing with milk and honey.” (Jeremiah 32:22) God made the promise, and God gave the land. I like when a promise comes with a delivery.

explanations.answer: A king to lead them into battle
explanations.explanation: A king isn't in Jeremiah's list here. After Egypt, he says God gave them the land He had sworn to give their fathers (Jeremiah 32:22). Land is the gift in this verse, friend, not a leader.

explanations.answer: A city with high stone walls
explanations.explanation: Jeremiah doesn't talk about a walled city in this verse. He says God gave them “…a land flowing with milk and honey.” (Jeremiah 32:22) It's the whole land that was promised to their fathers, not one city.

Jeremiah says the opposite, friend. He says, “They came in and possessed it, but they did not obey Your voice or walk in Your law.” (Jeremiah 32:23) They got the land, but not the listening. That's the hard part of this prayer.

That's right, baker. Jeremiah says they possessed the land, “but they did not obey Your voice or walk in Your law.” (Jeremiah 32:23) The promise was kept on God's side. It's a heavy line, so we'll let it sit.

Jeremiah says they did not do all God commanded, “…and so You have brought upon them all this disaster.” (Jeremiah 32:23) He's looking right at it while he prays, since the siege is outside. Disaster is the word he uses, so that's the word we keep.
Darkness is a good guess for a heavy moment, baker, but it isn't Jeremiah's word. He says God brought “…all this disaster” on them (Jeremiah 32:23). The verse sticks to disaster.

Confusion isn't the word in this verse, friend. Jeremiah says that because they did not do what God commanded, “…You have brought upon them all this disaster.” (Jeremiah 32:23) The siege outside was nothing like a mix-up. That's why the word is disaster.

Jeremiah points at the siege and says, “What You have spoken has happened, as You now see!” (Jeremiah 32:24) The ramps are up and the Chaldeans, the Babylonians, are fighting against the city. God spoke, and here it is. Jeremiah isn't arguing with it, baker. He's telling God what he sees.

Jeremiah says the opposite, friend. He looks at the siege ramps and the Chaldeans, the Babylonians, and says, “What You have spoken has happened, as You now see!” (Jeremiah 32:24) The words happened, and he says so out loud.

Jeremiah says God told him, “Buy for yourself the field with silver and call in witnesses…” (Jeremiah 32:25) Silver, plus people watching to make it official. Think of it as a signed receipt, with people there to say they saw it. Even with the city handed over, God's instructions on the field stayed the same.

Planting isn't in the order, baker. Jeremiah says God told him, “Buy for yourself the field with silver and call in witnesses…” (Jeremiah 32:25) The order is about buying it and having witnesses. Nobody's handing him a bag of seeds.

Selling it back isn't part of what God told him, friend. Jeremiah quotes God: “Buy for yourself the field with silver and call in witnesses…” (Jeremiah 32:25) Buy it, and call the witnesses. Nothing about a return policy.

explanations.answer: Set it on fire and burn it
explanations.explanation: God says the Chaldeans, the Babylonians, will come in, set the city on fire and burn it (Jeremiah 32:29). It's a hard line, and I think it's one to read slowly. God says it plainly, so we hear it plainly.

explanations.answer: Leave it standing and go home
explanations.explanation: That's not what God says. He says the Chaldeans, the Babylonians, will come in, set the city on fire and burn it (Jeremiah 32:29). They don't just walk in, look around and head home, baker.

A new capital isn't in the verse, friend. God says the Chaldeans, who are fighting against the city, will come in, set it on fire and burn it (Jeremiah 32:29). Burned and moved into aren't the same thing.

God says some of those houses belong to people who provoked Him to anger “…by burning incense to Baal on their rooftops…” (Jeremiah 32:29). Baal was a false god. The verse also says they poured out drink offerings to other gods.

That's not in this verse, baker. God says they provoked Him to anger “…by burning incense to Baal on their rooftops and by pouring out drink offerings to other gods.” (Jeremiah 32:29) Baal was a false god. Both of the things He names are about worshiping false gods.

Treaties aren't mentioned here, friend. God says the houses belong to those who provoked Him “…by burning incense to Baal on their rooftops and by pouring out drink offerings to other gods.” (Jeremiah 32:29) Baal was a false god. The offerings are what He names.
God says, “Therefore I will remove it from My presence…” (Jeremiah 32:31). It's serious. I think this one lands heavy, and we don't need to dress it up.

That isn't what God says here, baker. He says, “Therefore I will remove it from My presence…” (Jeremiah 32:31). The warnings are already behind them, because He says He taught them again and again (Jeremiah 32:33).

Not quite, friend. God says, “Therefore I will remove it from My presence…” (Jeremiah 32:31), and earlier He says the city will be set on fire and burned (Jeremiah 32:29). That's not a leave-it-standing kind of ending.

God says the opposite, baker. He includes the leaders too: “…they, their kings, their officials, their priests and prophets, the men of Judah, and the residents of Jerusalem.” (Jeremiah 32:32) Kings, priests and prophets are right there on the list. Nobody's sitting this one out.

That's right, friend. God names everybody, kings and officials, priests and prophets, the men of Judah and the residents of Jerusalem (Jeremiah 32:32). The list is long on purpose, I think. It's a sober line, so we'll take it as it is.

God says, “They have turned their backs to Me and not their faces.” (Jeremiah 32:33) That's a picture anyone gets. Nobody has to explain what it means to be turned away from. He keeps teaching, but they won't turn around to listen.

You're close on the idea, since the same verse says they would not listen. But the word God uses is “backs”: “They have turned their backs to Me and not their faces.” (Jeremiah 32:33) It's about which way they're facing, friend.
Hands aren't the word in this verse, baker. God says, “They have turned their backs to Me and not their faces.” (Jeremiah 32:33) Backs, not hands. It's the picture of someone facing the other way.

explanations.answer: In the house that bears His Name
explanations.explanation: God says, “They have placed their abominations in the house that bears My Name, and so have defiled it.” (Jeremiah 32:34) That's the very house with His Name on it. I think that's what makes this line sting.

explanations.answer: In the courtyard of the palace
explanations.explanation: A palace courtyard isn't in this verse, friend. God says, “They have placed their abominations in the house that bears My Name, and so have defiled it.” (Jeremiah 32:34) The house that bears His Name is the place He names.

explanations.answer: Beside the gates of the city
explanations.explanation: Gates aren't mentioned here, baker. God says they placed their abominations “…in the house that bears My Name, and so have defiled it.” (Jeremiah 32:34) It's the house with His own Name on it.

God says it was “…something I never commanded them, nor had it ever entered My mind, that they should commit such an abomination and cause Judah to sin.” (Jeremiah 32:35) This is a heavy part, baker, about sons and daughters passing through the fire to Molech, a false god. So no jokes here. God says it never came from Him.

God says the opposite, friend. He says it was “…something I never commanded them, nor had it ever entered My mind…” (Jeremiah 32:35) It's about the sons and daughters passed through the fire to Molech, a false god. I think this one hurts, so I'll leave it there.

explanations.answer: Gather them from all the lands
explanations.explanation: God says, “I will surely gather My people from all the lands to which I have banished them…” (Jeremiah 32:37). After all that burning talk, listen to that turn. He says He will gather them, and He says it with surely. That's how we know the story isn't over.

explanations.answer: Leave them in Babylon for good
explanations.explanation: Not at all, baker. God says, “I will surely gather My people from all the lands to which I have banished them…” (Jeremiah 32:37). Banished is only half of what He says. He goes on to say He will return them to this place.
That's the opposite of what God says, friend. He says, “I will surely gather My people from all the lands to which I have banished them…” (Jeremiah 32:37). Gather is the word, not scatter.

God says it plainly: “They will be My people, and I will be their God.” (Jeremiah 32:38) Short and simple, and it's the heart of the whole promise. After everything He just said, this is where He lands, baker.

God says exactly this, friend: “They will be My people, and I will be their God.” (Jeremiah 32:38) It comes right after the hard words about the city. The promise is that they are His and He is theirs.

explanations.answer: Always fear Him for their good
explanations.explanation: God says He will give them one heart and one way, “…so that they will always fear Me for their own good and for the good of their children after them.” (Jeremiah 32:39) It's good for them, and good for their children after them. Notice how far ahead He's looking.

explanations.answer: Rebuild the walls of the city
explanations.explanation: Walls aren't in this promise, baker. God says He will give them one heart and one way, “…so that they will always fear Me for their own good and for the good of their children after them.” (Jeremiah 32:39) The promise is about their hearts.

Ruling over neighbors isn't what God says, friend. He gives them one heart and one way, “…so that they will always fear Me for their own good and for the good of their children after them.” (Jeremiah 32:39) It's a promise about hearts and children.

God says, “I will put My fear in their hearts, so that they will never turn away from Me.” (Jeremiah 32:40) Remember Jeremiah's prayer, where the people turned their backs. Here God says He will put His fear in their hearts so it won't happen again. He's doing the heart work Himself.
Envy isn't named in this verse, baker. God says He will put His fear in their hearts, “…so that they will never turn away from Me.” (Jeremiah 32:40) The promise is about not turning away from Him.

Tribes fighting isn't in this verse, friend. God says, “I will put My fear in their hearts, so that they will never turn away from Me.” (Jeremiah 32:40) The thing it keeps them from is turning away from Him.

God says the opposite, baker. He says, “Just as I have brought all this great disaster on this people, so I will bring on them all the good I have promised them.” (Jeremiah 32:42) He used the word all for the disaster, and He uses all again for the good. No half portions here.
That's right, friend. God says, “…so I will bring on them all the good I have promised them.” (Jeremiah 32:42) Just as the disaster was real, the good will be too. All of it.

God says, “And fields will be bought in this land about which you are saying, ‘It is a desolation, without man or beast…’” (Jeremiah 32:43). That's the same kind of deal Jeremiah just made. His purchase was a sign of what God says is coming.
Horses aren't the thing being bought, baker. God says, “And fields will be bought in this land…” (Jeremiah 32:43). It's fields, like the one Jeremiah bought.
No weapons here, friend. God says, “And fields will be bought in this land…” (Jeremiah 32:43). In a land people called desolate, folks buying fields is a pretty peaceful picture.

explanations.answer: He will restore them from captivity
explanations.explanation: God says it will happen “…because I will restore them from captivity, declares the LORD.” (Jeremiah 32:44) The reason is Him. He's the one who restores. The field Jeremiah bought is the first one, and this is why more are coming.

explanations.answer: Babylon will lose interest in the land
explanations.explanation: That's not the reason God gives, baker. He says fields will be bought “…because I will restore them from captivity, declares the LORD.” (Jeremiah 32:44) It all rests on what God will do, not on what Babylon feels.

explanations.answer: The people will earn the land back
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say that, friend. God says fields will be bought “…because I will restore them from captivity, declares the LORD.” (Jeremiah 32:44) The restoring is His work. Earning isn't the word in this verse.
